profiles.meeting_scenario: A midweek coordination meeting for the staff supporting a large undergraduate software engineering capstone course that is structured as 20-person 'companies' building a shared microservices product. One staff workstream maintains the platform contract package and coaches the student Platform sub-team; the other runs course-wide integration operations for the upcoming cross-company plug-and-play exercise. By Friday, each company must expose compatible APIs and deploy services to the shared staging environment so a partner company can integrate against them with minimal live support. The agenda is to align on what Platform will hand off, what being deployed to staging for the integration check entails, how readiness and blockers will be reflected in the shared coordination artifacts, and what level of plug-and-play compatibility other companies should be able to rely on. The expected outcome is that both staff members leave believing they have aligned on the API artifact to freeze, the staging handoff, use of the integration board as the source of truth, and the scope of Friday compatibility.

members.name: Nina Patel
members.expertise: Backend engineering, API design, student team coaching, Docker-based development workflows
members.background: Senior master's student who previously interned on a microservices platform team and now supervises the student Platform sub-team responsible for auth, gateway conventions, and the reference contract package used across the capstone companies.
members.private_state: She wants to protect her students from late contract churn and avoid reopening edge-case discussions this close to the event; she is also aware the human-facing docs are slightly behind and hopes the tagged contract bundle will be treated as sufficient.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the API spec,' they mean the versioned OpenAPI bundle in the platform-contracts repository tagged for the sprint, because that is the artifact clients and tests are generated from.

If a service is deployed to staging for the integration check, the point of the check is interface compatibility in the shared environment, so mocked downstream services are acceptable as long as endpoints are reachable through the gateway.
If the integration board is the source of truth for blockers, the integration coordinator's workflow is to collect updates from leads and record or normalize them centrally.
Being 'plug-and-play compatible' for Friday means another company can authenticate, call the main happy-path flows, and get contract-conformant responses without negotiating endpoint shapes live.
Small mismatches in wiki examples or unfinalized error semantics do not threaten Friday if the tagged contract bundle and gateway behavior are stable.

members.name: Owen Morales
members.expertise: Release coordination, CI/CD pipelines, staging operations, cross-team dependency tracking
members.background: Lecturer and former DevOps engineer who oversees the shared staging cluster, the cross-company integration exercise, and the dashboards and boards staff use to judge whether student companies are genuinely ready to interoperate.
members.private_state: He wants Friday to run without staff doing ad hoc interpretation for students, and he worries teams often claim readiness based on demoable slices rather than operationally representative behavior; he also wants workstream leads to update their own status so the shared board stays current without manual chasing.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the API spec,' they mean the latest course-facing contract page and example payloads that external student companies will actually read during setup, even if those examples are derived from a repo artifact.

If a service is deployed to staging for the integration check, the check is the standard smoke run in a realistic shared environment, so real internal dependencies should be wired unless explicitly exempted.
If the integration board is the source of truth for blockers, each workstream lead is expected to enter and maintain their own readiness notes, dependency flags, and compatibility caveats directly.
Being 'plug-and-play compatible' means another company can use the published setup notes and smoke cases, including error-handling and pagination expectations, without coordinator intervention.
Students treat the wiki and board as operational truth during integration, so anything not reflected there is effectively unavailable to partner teams.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to freezing or handing off 'the API spec' for Friday's plug-and-play event.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the tagged OpenAPI bundle in the platform-contracts repository, specifically the sprint tag students use for code generation and contract validation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the course-facing wiki contract page with example payloads and compatibility notes that partner companies actually consult during integration.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts usually move together and describe the same endpoints, so 'the API spec' feels like a single obvious thing; each person assumes the other's role naturally points to the same artifact and sees no reason to disambiguate.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'deployed to staging for the integration check' implies
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the services need to be 'deployed to staging for the integration check' before Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 takes the integration check to mean interface validation in the shared staging environment, so deployment is sufficient if the service is reachable through the gateway and can use mocked downstream dependencies.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 takes the integration check to mean the standard end-to-end smoke run in staging, so deployment is sufficient only if real internal dependencies are wired and the normal smoke path works without mocks.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like ordinary release coordination language centered on a goal rather than mechanics, and both believe the purpose of the check is already obvious from the course context, so the hidden threshold difference never gets verbalized.

misalignment_points.topic: How the integration board becomes the source of truth
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to use 'the integration board as the source of truth for blockers' ahead of the cross-company session.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes she will mention blockers or contract changes in staff syncs or messages and the integration operation will enter and maintain the board fields centrally.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes M1, as the workstream lead, will directly update the board lane, blocker status, and compatibility notes for Platform herself.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They are aligned on the board's purpose rather than explicitly discussing the act of updating it; because the board already exists and both endorse it, the missing procedural ownership feels too mundane to spell out.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both describe the Platform services as needing to be 'plug-and-play compatible' with the partner company by Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes stable endpoint shapes, auth headers, and successful happy-path behavior for the main gateway flows another company will demo first.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes those items plus published error responses, pagination defaults, and the smoke-test cases the partner company is expected to run unassisted.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The course slogan is familiar and sounds like shared doctrine, so both hear confirmation of the same broad goal; the omitted boundary details feel like obvious implementation-level consequences rather than something needing explicit negotiation.
